citation: Xie L, Chen J, Dai J, et al. (2024). Exploring the potent enhancement effects of plyometric training on vertical jumping and sprinting ability in sports individuals. Frontiers in Physiology.
population: Athletes with ≥1 year sports experience (293 participants: 163 males, 21 females, 109 gender not reported)
intervention: Plyometric training (post-activation potentiation/PAP training) in various forms: single vs complex, single-session vs multiple-session, with rest intervals categorized as short (0.3–4 min), moderate (5–7 min), and long (>8 min)
summary: This meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (293 athletes) examined acute effects of plyometric training on vertical jump and sprint performance. Single plyometric training showed a small positive effect on vertical jump (SMD = −0.24) with optimal rest intervals of 0.3–4 min, while complex plyometric training yielded a moderate effect on vertical jump (SMD = 0.58) with best results at rest intervals >8 min. Sprint performance improved slightly after single training (SMD = 0.27) and substantially after complex training (SMD = 0.80).
key_findings: Single plyometric training on vertical jump: SMD = −0.24, 95% CI (−0.38, −0.10), P = 0.0009 (small effect).
Optimal rest interval for single plyometric training on vertical jump: 0.3–4 min, SMD = 0.30, P = 0.0008.
Complex plyometric training on vertical jump: SMD = 0.58, 95% CI (−0.86, −0.23), P = 0.002 (moderate effect), with largest effect at rest >8 min (|SMD| = 0.77).
Single plyometric training on sprint: SMD = 0.27, 95% CI (0.03, 0.52), P = 0.03 (small effect).
Complex plyometric training on sprint: SMD = 0.80, 95% CI (0.01, 1.59), P = 0.05 (large effect), but with high heterogeneity (I² = 85%).
effect_size: Single PAP vertical jump: SMD = −0.24, 95% CI (−0.38, −0.10); Complex PAP vertical jump: SMD = 0.58, 95% CI (−0.86, −0.23); Single PAP sprint: SMD = 0.27, 95% CI (0.03, 0.52); Complex PAP sprint: SMD = 0.80, 95% CI (0.01, 1.59)
limitations: High heterogeneity in complex plyometric training analyses (I² up to 85%); publication bias detected for some subgroups; limited number of studies for sprint outcomes (only 5 studies for complex PAP); gender not reported for 37% of participants.
